doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Personnel of the Naval Pre-Flight band
summary: He lists Marshall and Ernie Royal, Vernon Alley, Baranco, Curtis Lowe, Jerome Richardson, Jackie Kelso and Buddy Collette's second band.

His brother, Ernie Royal, outstanding trumpet player who ended up in New York doing studio work, but they all were with the original Lionel Hampton band, the band that made “Flying Home.” Vernon Alley of course, Mister Music, he was in the band, Wilbert Baranco, who is mentioned in the Leonard Feather, who was a very fine musician/pianist/singer and arranger. Wilbert, during the WPA days, he had been connected with the music project in San Francisco, and he wrote for everything, orchestra, voices, strings. And prior to that he had been on the road with — oh what the heck, the name slips but it will come to me in a moment — but Wilbert was a very, very fine pianist and arranger. Then we had Ernie Royal, we had Herman Grimes, a fine trumpet player who had played in Los Angeles with Les Hite and some of the other bands. Ike Bill out of Kansas City who grew up with Basie and all the Kansas City bunch. Trombones Dan Hamilton, Frasier Scott and Ralph Bledsoe, who was a very, very fine arranger and trombonist. He later became a dentist. And on saxophones you had Curtis Lowe, baritone. Curtis and I, well we knew one another like I say from 1937. Curtis later, after the Navy band, we went together around here and then he left and went with Lionel Hampton and then he was back and forth with Lionel Hampton and Curtis ended up working at the musicians’ union at our Local 669 as the secretary. Then when we merged he was given a job as assistant to Local 6 and they welcomed him because he had gained so much knowledge of Federation rules and he was a marvel with wage scales and things. Then we had Q. Dullis Martin, he played tenor sax, clarinet and arranged. He had been with the Les Hite band in Los Angeles and also with the Benny Carter band. And Q, he could write arrangements just like you were writing a letter. Then we had Jerome Richardson, he was on alto and flute. Then we had Jackie Kelson. He’s now the lead alto player with the new Basie Band. Yeah, Jack Kelson. And Andy Anderson on tenor sax. Andy was from Cleveland, a very fine saxophone player. He didn’t achieve any really notoriety or didn’t become a big name but he was an outstanding player. Now this is our Naval Pre-Flight band. Benny Sexton played guitar, an excellent guitarist, and I already mentioned Vernon on the bass. Then we had Buddy Collette. Buddy Collette was in the band. And Marshall wanted him to be in the number one dance band. But Buddy declined and so what happened, out of the 45 men, Marshall took the cream. So Buddy took the other guys, and whipped them into a band. We were the Rhythm Bombardiers, and I’ve forgotten for the moment what Buddy called his band. Anyhow he whipped them into such good shape that they would go out and play for dances at the USO on the various places, just like we would, as the number one band. But they were the names, and people who went on to become further in their career. We had other fellows in there, but — out of 45 men — and their names slip me for the moment.
